cues.text: Section eleven.
Practical lesson: Infrastructure as Code and automated policy enforcement.
Let us begin with the core idea.
Infrastructure as Code, or IaC, represents infrastructure requirements in machine-readable configuration.
Instead of manually requesting and configuring servers, teams submit declarative specifications to automated provisioning systems.
This improves repeatability and speed, but it comes with a caution: it can rapidly reproduce unsafe configurations.
Whatever is written in the specification, good or bad, can be created again and again very quickly.
That is where shift-left security comes in.
Shift-left security introduces checks before deployment, rather than waiting until a system is already running.
Closely related is policy as code, which expresses organisational rules in executable form.
A validation gate then rejects configurations that violate mandatory requirements.
In this way, the business's risk tolerance is connected directly to engineering decisions.
Now consider an independent teaching example.
It uses Python to check three things: encryption, public SSH exposure and backups.
The code defines a function called validate, which takes a configuration.
Inside it, it starts with an empty list called violations.
Then it applies three checks in turn.
First, if the configuration's encrypted value is not exactly True, it adds the message "Storage encryption required" to the violations list.
Second, if port 22 appears in the configuration's list of public ports, it adds "Public SSH prohibited".
If the key public ports is missing, the code falls back to an empty list, so nothing is flagged.
Third, if the backup value is not exactly True, it adds "Automated backups required".
Finally, the function returns two things: whether there are no violations, which is True only when the list is empty, and the list of violations itself.
Below the function, two sample configurations are defined.
The safe one has encryption set to True, public ports containing only 443, and backup set to True.
The unsafe one has encryption set to False, public ports containing 22 and 443, and backup set to False.
The code then prints the result of validating each.
The expected result is as follows.
The safe configuration returns True with an empty list.
The unsafe configuration returns False, together with three violations: one for missing encryption, one for public SSH, and one for missing backups.
This is a teaching example, so it is deliberately small.
In a real pipeline, several further elements are also necessary: schema validation, authenticated policy changes, logging, exception handling, and enforcement against actual deployed infrastructure.
One more point is worth noting.
A port number alone does not establish whether access is public, which is why the example explicitly models public ports as its own field.
To close this lab, notice what it demonstrates: alignment.
The business needs trustworthy financial services.
Governance defines the mandatory controls.
And automated engineering enforces those controls consistently before provisioning.
